questions.stem: A converging lens is one which

options.text: is thinner at the centre than at the edges and spreads a parallel beam
is thicker at the centre than at the edges and brings a parallel beam to a real focus
has a virtual principal focus on the same side as the incident light
always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image

questions.explanation: A converging (convex) lens is thicker in the middle. Parallel rays are refracted towards the principal axis and actually meet at a real principal focus on the far side of the lens, so the focal length is taken as positive under the real-is-positive convention.

distractorRationale.a: Thinner at the centre describes a diverging (concave) lens, which spreads a parallel beam
distractorRationale.c: A virtual focus on the incident-light side belongs to a diverging lens
distractorRationale.d: Always virtual, erect and diminished is the image formed by a diverging lens, not a converging one

questions.stem: A student who cannot see distant objects clearly is suffering from myopia. The defect is corrected with
questions.explanation: In myopia (short-sightedness) the uncorrected eye focuses a distant object in front of the retina. A diverging (concave) lens spreads the incoming rays slightly so that the eye's own lens can then bring them to a focus on the retina. The spectacle lens therefore has a negative power.

distractorRationale.a: A converging lens is used for hypermetropia (long-sightedness), where the image would otherwise form behind the retina
distractorRationale.c: A cylindrical lens corrects astigmatism, not ordinary myopia
distractorRationale.d: Plane glass does not change the convergence of the beam, so it cannot move the image onto the retina

questions.stem: An object is placed beyond 2F in front of a thin convex lens. The image formed is

options.text: real, inverted and diminished, between F and 2F
virtual, erect and magnified, on the same side as the object
real, inverted and the same size, at 2F

questions.explanation: For a convex lens, an object beyond 2F produces a real inverted image that lies between F and 2F and is smaller than the object. This is the camera arrangement: a large distant scene is reduced onto the film. The magnified real image appears only when the object is between F and 2F, and the virtual erect image only when the object is closer than F.

distractorRationale.b: Real, inverted and magnified beyond 2F is the image when the object itself is between F and 2F
distractorRationale.c: Virtual, erect and magnified is the magnifying-glass case, with the object between F and the lens
distractorRationale.d: Same-size image at 2F occurs only when the object is itself at 2F

questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance. Give your answer in centimetres.
questions.explanation: Using the real-is-positive convention, $f = +10\ \text{cm}$ and $u = 30\ \text{cm}$. From $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}$ we get $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{15}$, so $v = 15\ \text{cm}$. The positive sign means the image is real and on the opposite side of the lens from the object.

questions.stem: The linear magnification $m$ produced by a lens is given by
questions.explanation: Linear magnification is the ratio of image height to object height. Similar triangles in the ray diagram show that this ratio equals image distance over object distance, so $m = \frac{h_i}{h_o} = \frac{v}{u}$. A value of $m > 1$ means a magnified image; $m < 1$ means a diminished image.

distractorRationale.a: This is the reciprocal of the magnification; using it would swap object and image sizes
distractorRationale.c: u + v is a length, not a ratio, and has no meaning as magnification
distractorRationale.d: 1/f is the power of the lens in dioptres when f is in metres, not the magnification

questions.stem: A converging lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Calculate its power in dioptres.
questions.explanation: Power is $P = \frac{1}{f}$ with $f$ in metres. Convert 20 cm to 0.20 m. The lens is converging, so $f$ is positive: $P = \frac{1}{0.20} = +5.0\ \text{D}$. Leaving f in centimetres would give 0.05, which is not the power in dioptres.

questions.stem: The power of a thin diverging lens of focal length 25 cm is
questions.explanation: A diverging lens has a virtual focus, so $f = -25\ \text{cm} = -0.25\ \text{m}$. Then $P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{-0.25} = -4.0\ \text{D}$. Both the conversion to metres and the negative sign are required; missing either one produces one of the distractors.

distractorRationale.a: This is the magnitude of the power with the wrong sign — the sign that belongs to a converging lens of the same |f|
distractorRationale.c: This is 1/25 with f left in centimetres and the sign dropped
distractorRationale.d: This treats f as −0.04 m, or equivalently takes P = f in centimetres with a negative sign

questions.stem: An object 4.0 cm high is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The image is
questions.explanation: From $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{30}$, so $v = +30\ \text{cm}$. The image is real. Magnification $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{30}{15} = 2.0$, so $h_i = 2.0 \times 4.0 = 8.0\ \text{cm}$ and the image is inverted. The object lies between F (10 cm) and 2F (20 cm), which independently confirms a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F.

distractorRationale.b: A virtual erect image would require the object to be closer than F (u < 10 cm); here u = 15 cm, so the image is real
distractorRationale.c: This uses m = u/v = 1/2 instead of v/u, giving a diminished image of 2.0 cm
distractorRationale.d: This is the arithmetic mean of object and image distances used as a height, which has no physical basis

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about a diverging lens?

options.text: It causes parallel rays of light to converge.
It has a negative focal length.
It can magnify objects larger than their actual size.

questions.explanation: A diverging lens, also known as a concave lens, has a negative focal length because it causes light rays to spread out or diverge. This characteristic is essential for understanding how images are formed by such lenses.

distractorRationale.a: This describes a converging lens, not a diverging lens.
distractorRationale.b: Diverging lenses always produce virtual images, not real ones.
distractorRationale.d: Diverging lenses produce diminished images, not larger ones.

questions.stem: What is the lens formula for a thin lens?
questions.explanation: The lens formula for a thin lens relates the focal length (f), the image distance (v), and the object distance (u) with the equation 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. This formula is crucial for solving lens problems.

distractorRationale.b: This is not the correct relationship; it does not represent the lens formula.
distractorRationale.c: This equation does not apply to lenses; it is incorrect.
distractorRationale.d: This is a misrepresentation of the lens formula.

questions.stem: If an object is placed at the focal point of a converging lens, what type of image is formed?
questions.explanation: When an object is placed at the focal point of a converging lens, the rays of light emerge parallel and thus form an image at infinity. This concept is important in optics and helps in understanding lens behavior.

distractorRationale.a: An image cannot be real and inverted when the object is at the focal point.
distractorRationale.b: The image is not virtual; it is formed at infinity.
distractorRationale.d: An image is formed, but it is not at a finite distance.

questions.stem: A convex lens has a focal length of 15 cm. What is its power in dioptres?
questions.explanation: The power of a lens is calculated using the formula P = 1/f (in meters). For a focal length of 15 cm (0.15 m), the power is P = 1/0.15 = +6.67 D, indicating that it is a converging lens.

distractorRationale.b: This value is incorrect; it does not follow the formula for power.
distractorRationale.c: The power cannot be negative for a converging lens.
distractorRationale.d: This value is far too low; it does not represent the correct calculation.

questions.stem: What is the magnification produced by a lens if the image distance is 20 cm and the object distance is 10 cm?
questions.explanation: Magnification (m) is calculated using the formula m = v/u. Here, v = 20 cm and u = 10 cm, thus m = 20/10 = 2. This means the image is twice the size of the object.

distractorRationale.a: This value indicates a smaller image, which is incorrect in this case.
distractorRationale.b: This would mean the image size is equal to the object size, which is not applicable here.
distractorRationale.d: This value suggests an even larger image, which does not match the given distances.

questions.stem: Which type of lens is used to correct hyperopia?
questions.explanation: Hyperopia, or farsightedness, is corrected using a convex lens, which helps to converge light rays before they enter the eye, allowing for clearer vision of nearby objects.

distractorRationale.b: A concave lens is used to correct myopia, not hyperopia.
distractorRationale.c: Bifocal lenses are used for presbyopia, not specifically for hyperopia.
distractorRationale.d: Cylindrical lenses are used for astigmatism, not hyperopia.

distractorRationale.b: This is incorrect as it does not match the calculated image distance.
distractorRationale.c: This suggests a real image, which is not possible with a concave lens for this situation.
distractorRationale.d: This value is incorrect as it does not reflect the correct calculation.

distractorRationale.c: Power cannot remain constant if focal length changes.
distractorRationale.d: Power is positive for converging lenses and negative for diverging lenses, but this does not directly relate to focal length increase.
